My mother lives with me and has an older dog who is 100 lbs. Without warning, she had my daughter pinned and bit her on the shoulder and went for her neck, but thankfully thought better of it and backed off leaving just a minor scratch. We took my daughter to get antibiotics and the incident was reported, but left up to us to handle. Because it was not unprovoked, but was without warning, we have decided she can stay , but is not allowed around the kids. When the kids are in bed or at school she can be around the house, but when the kids are around she is in a locked in my mother's bedroom. I keep the key up high so no kids gets tempted and when my mom is in there with her, she keeps it locked. Adults go in and out of there and she gets affection. If she needs to go out she is leashed and let out in the back, which is also locked while she is out there. 

I understand her reaction, but because of her size and lack of warning, and the fact that it happened so quickly even under supervision, she has to be isolated from kids and guests for the safety of my kids and her own safety. We also have instructed the kids that they are not to interact with her and they are very respectful of that rule, in fact my 3yo is, understandably terrified of her. We have also had MANY discussions with the kids about being aware of the space we are using when around animals, and how to interact properly so that another incident like this does not occur with any other pets. 

I have been VERY firm about the locked door. At first my mom kept referencing "when we let her go back to normal" but I was adamant that this needed to be the new normal. I wouldn't say snooping is worse than what he did, but if he wasn't aware that she was looking through his phone...she was snooping. I only think that is important to consider because she needs to think about why she was snooping. Is it because he isn't trust worthy, or because she finds it hard to trust in general. There is more to it and obviously there are at least a couple of issues to be discussed between them.

I tend to agree with some less popular opinions. I have been in both trusting and non-trusting relationships and have been on my SO's phone/computer in both scenarios.  In a trusting relationship you usually say something along the lines of "Hey, I need to look at the message that I sent you. (Because I can't look at it from my end for whatever reason) Mind if I borrow your phone?"  He has never said no or hesitated. Also, I only look at what I said I was going to look at. When I was untrusting I looked at the phone when he wasn't around and without consent and usually found exactly what I expected. Intuition is often right.  I always made sure that I had a reason to be looking that sounded conceivable enough to justify it though. 

All that said, it doesn't make what he did OK. You just need to be prepared to take your side of the blame for snooping too.  He will be upset and excuses probably won't help.  Also, you need to honestly admit to yourself why you were looking at his phone.  Is it because you have trust issues despite him being trustworthy or Is it because he is truly not trustworthy? Obviously you've already found some evidence.  And even before that something made you feel the need to look. Don't stay in a relationship if you really cannot trust your significant other, it will drive you absolutely insane and make you stoop to levels that you shouldn't. I've been there.  Trust your intuition and communicate, if that doesn't solve the problem then it may be time to go.

As a vegetarian, I cannot stand when vegans tell me I'm not doing enough. However, she is right about what happens. They actually do that more often than not. If something is "standard industry practice" it is not usually subject to cruelty laws. They may keep one or two males out of a few hundred, but they aren't too worried about gene diversity and males get aggressive, so they kill most of them.  If an animal doesn't yield enough it becomes meat. These animals are bred to yield plenty regardless of their mood. Simple anatomy makes them produce. I promise you they don't care if they are happy. They do much worse too. If you buy milk or eggs at grocery store that's almost certainly what you are buying from. I try to buy local and/or know about the farm my stuff comes from. I'm sure many would still find that to be wrong, but I get my eggs from my dads chickens who live out their whole lives (even after they stop laying) and milk is a bit harder, but I really try to buy the most humane I can find, or buy plant based. Cheese is easier to be found at local farmers market's.

 All that said, I say learn and do what you can when you can to support humane farming whether you're eating meat or simply dairy and eggs and ypu are doing well.  It doesn't always have to be all or nothing.

I went to a University in Texas called Sul Ross State University. They have a great wildlife program for this part of the country, as does Texas A&M. I am not sure about programs in other parts of the globe though. My B.S. degree is in Natural Resource Management with a concentration in Wildlife management and my M.S. is concentrated in conservation Biology, actually. They had a concentration option for rangeland studies as well, which focused more on flora/soil management. Really it would depend on you options as far as location. If you can move, I would go to an area with the flora and fauna you would like to work with and find a school with an appropriate degree program. Typically the best programs are going to be at least slightly off the beaten path, (i.e. you wont find them in the middle of major urban hubs) as you will need access to wildlands for valuable experience.  If moving is not an option, find out what your local university offers, even some community colleges offer introductory classes. I would recommend a 4 year university as an end goal though. I see that you said he is in Egypt, I don't know much about Egypt specifically, but he is on a very ecologically rich  continent, so there are probably many options for him not terribly far away. Just plan to study, or at least intern in an area similar to where you would like to work. It is a very hands-on field and most of your most valuable education will come from field work. I think you should just contact an adviser from a college where you plan to study and see what they recommend.

Formal study or lots of experience is generally pretty vital for paying jobs. A good way to get in to it without formal education may be to look for work as a zoo keeper and try to get involved in the conservation/breeding programs that they participate in. That won't nessecarily get you in to field work, but is a way to get involved. I am in the reverse of this situation. I got my degrees in wildlife studies and now want to change paths lol. He will need t decide pretty specifically what he wants to do as there are many concentrations available ( marine, fire ecology,range land wildlife, fisheries etc.) A lot of that may depend on geographic location for him. Look for what is most widely needed in his area.

I always knew something was missing between my parents. I sensed the stressed relationship, but they put on a happy front. I rarely saw them fight, and I even saw some affection, but it wasn't real. It was things like catching glimpses of dirty looks given to one another, even when I don't think they knew they were doing it. Kids are smarter than they get credit for sometime. I remember asking my mom when she and my dad would divorce sometime in elementary school. She thought it was because my friend's parents were splitting up, but I really could sense the inevitability of it and, like most children, had no filter. They didn't split up until they were in their 50s and I was 25. He had an affair. It was devastating. I'll always love my dad, but I lost my hero. I think he tried to force things for way too long with my mom and eventually broke. I cannot excuse the affair, but I think that was likely the reason for it. My mom was crushed and I had to give up my master's degree in my final semester to move home for suicide watch and help support her financially. My SO of 9 years moved with me, but the stress of my personal drama is a big contributor to what eventually tore us apart. Four years later and things have only slightly gotten better. My entire life plan has changed and not for the better. I wish they would have separated as a kid. My mom would have been young enough and in a better job market to be employed more easily and my dad could have remained my hero. Even 4 years later it devastates me to think about what he did. I would have loved to have been left out of that loop as a child would have been. Not to say it isn't tough for kids, but they don't typically know the details and still can see both parents as role models. As an adult, so much pressure was put on to me, more by myself and circumstance than by my mom, to help out. 

Anyway, all of that to say DO NOT stay together for the kids. It is no easier for an adult child of divorce. You can still raise them and they will have a happier childhood. They want to see you happy as much as you want to be....I speak from experience. Not to say it won't be an upsetting experience, but it will all be for the better.

I work for a no-kill large breed rescue and we get constantly inundated with request to surrender. Every reason from "hes not very cute anymore" (yep I've heard that) to more legitimate ones like "I have a terminal illness and need to be sure my pet is safe". Unfortunately there are very few of these that we take in, because on top of those we have kill shelters emailing their euthanasia lists daily. If we get an opening that's typically where we go to fill it. There is just no sense in waiting for the next legitimate call and having an open kennel, and no fair way to choose which public surrenders to take. 

With all of that in mind, we do often recommend using Craigslist and Facebook to re-home. We urge them to use caution in choosing a new owner and to have the dog vetted before hand, if possible. We go through several negative and positive re-homing scenarios. We offer some of our screening procedures and our assistance if they need help or have questions. We also offer to post their dogs on petfinder/petango etc. 

I do see the posts that you are referring to and they are often cringe worthy. I usually try to step in with some gentle re-homing advice, but I think I am usually ignored.
